ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, it is a composite image of stroboscopic photographs of Galileo's inclined-plane experiment done by modern people in a laboratory. In the experiment, a small ball is released from rest from a certain position on the left inclined plane, and it will rush up the right inclined plane. The stroboscopic photographs show that during the motion of the small ball on the right inclined plane, the distances between two adjacent small balls decrease in sequence; if the right inclined plane becomes horizontal, the stroboscopic photographs show that during the motion of the small ball on the right inclined plane, the distances between two adjacent small balls are almost equal. For this experiment, which of the following statements is correct ( )
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text: The above experiment shows that the conclusion that "if there were no frictional resistance, the small ball would move on the horizontal plane forever" is correct

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in the figure, in Galileo's inclined-plane experiment, if there were no frictional resistance, how would the small ball move on the horizontal plane?
ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_answer: The above experiment shows that the conclusion that "if there were no frictional resistance, the small ball would move on the horizontal plane forever" is correct.
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: The figure is a schematic/stroboscopic diagram of Galileo's inclined-plane experiment. On the left side there is a track inclined downward, and after the small ball slides from the left inclined plane to the bottom, it enters the track on the right; on the right side, tracks of different shapes are drawn, including an upward-inclined track and the lowermost horizontal track. In the figure, a series of white dots is used to represent the positions of the small ball at equal time intervals: on the upward inclined plane, the spacing between the small dots gradually becomes smaller, indicating that the small ball gradually slows down; on the horizontal track, the spacing between the small dots is almost equal. Then reason: Equal spacing of the stroboscopic dots indicates that the magnitude of the velocity of the small ball on the horizontal plane remains unchanged. The conditions in the question state that there is no frictional resistance, so on the horizontal plane there is no resistance that makes the small ball gradually slow down and stop. According to the law of inertia, the small ball will maintain its original state of motion and move in uniform straight-line motion on the horizontal plane, and will not stop by itself.
